name: RTL-SDR/LoRa/GPS/RTC HAT for Raspberry Pi
firmware: n/a (passive radio HAT; all processing on host Pi)
firmware_note: No onboard firmware layer - the HAT is a bundle of four independent radio front-ends (SDR, LoRa, GPS, RTC) that the Raspberry Pi's own OS and drivers (librtlsdr, Meshtastic, gpsd) talk to directly.
price_note: Preorder price at Hacker Gadgets; page listed an estimated ship date of 2026-09-20 at time of research. No independent reseller pricing found.
skill_note: Four separate radio subsystems each need their own host-side setup (librtlsdr, a Meshtastic/LoRa stack, gpsd) - nothing about it is plug-and-play beyond the physical HAT connection.
build_note: Assembled HAT that screws onto the Pi's 40-pin header; no soldering. Compatible with Pi 3B, 4B, 5, CM4, CM5, Zero and Zero 2W per the vendor.
summary: A Raspberry Pi HAT bundling a receive-only RTL2832U+R860 SDR tuner, a Semtech SX1262 LoRa radio (860-960 MHz with out-of-the-box Meshtastic support), a GNSS receiver, and a PCF85063A real-time clock with rechargeable coin-cell backup, aimed at turning a Pi into a self-contained spectrum-monitoring or mesh-relay station.
honest_take: This is four fairly ordinary radio modules sharing one PCB, not a unified 'signals platform.' The SDR side is receive-only - no DAC, no transmit path, so despite living in this batch it cannot do any of the sub-GHz transmit/replay/jamming work people associate with RF security gadgets. Its R860 tuner is functionally identical to the R820T2 found in $25 dongles (Rafael Micro simply renamed the die when R820T2 was formally discontinued) - it is not the three-port R828D used on the RTL-SDR Blog V4, and the advertised '100 kHz-28.8 MHz HF direct sampling' is the standard RTL2832U direct-sampling trick (bypassing the tuner entirely), not a dedicated HF upconverter, so expect the weaker sensitivity that comes with it. The LoRa and GPS/RTC sides are conventional and fine for a Meshtastic node. At $84.90 for four bundled radios you are paying hobbyist prices for hobbyist-grade parts; the appeal is integration and one shared enclosure, not superior performance versus buying an RTL-SDR dongle and a LoRa HAT separately.

summary: A receive-only 12-bit SDR in an aluminum case covering 10 kHz-2 GHz with up to 10 MHz of bandwidth, built on Mirics-family silicon - the same chip family SDRplay uses in its RSP line - and enumerating to the host as an SDRplay RSP1, so it runs SDRplay's own SDRuno/EXTIO software and anything else that speaks the RSP1 driver.
honest_take: Call this what independent reviewers already call it: a Chinese clone of the (now-discontinued) SDRplay RSP1, not an original design - it works because it uses Mirics chips and presents itself as the real thing over USB. It is genuinely good value on HF (reviewers found it close to indistinguishable from a real RSP1/RSP1A on shortwave), but it has 'very minimal filtering' compared to SDRplay's own current RSP1A, so expect more intermodulation and image problems on crowded bands without external filtering. It is also 12-bit, not the 14-bit ADC of the current SDRplay RSP1A (~$100, still in production, official support and firmware updates) - if you can stretch the extra ~$35, the genuine article gets you two more bits of dynamic range and a vendor who will answer support requests. None of your money reaches SDRplay when you buy this clone.

summary: A relay-switched HF upconverter and VHF/UHF preamp that sits between an antenna and an existing RTL-SDR/DVB-T dongle, shifting 10 kHz-50 MHz up into the dongle's normal tuning range while passing VHF/UHF/SHF straight through with a 3dB preamp.
honest_take: This is a classic mixer-based upconverter - the JasonKits listing does not name the exact IC, but this class of module has historically been built around an NE612/SA612-family mixer (now a legacy, out-of-production chip family per its Wikipedia entry, so modern boards may use a different but functionally similar part; unconfirmed here). It is not itself an SDR and does nothing without a separate RTL2832U-based dongle plugged downstream, which the listing explicitly states is 'NOT SUPPLIED.' It solves the exact HF problem the RTL-SDR Blog V4 already solves for free with a built-in SA612 upconverter - if you do not already own an older dongle that lacks HF coverage, buying a V4-class dongle instead is simpler and no more expensive than buying this plus a separate receive-only dongle.

name: PandwaRF Marauder
firmware: n/a (dedicated hardware, controlled via companion Android app)
price_note: First-pass seed price of $1,024 (sourced via reseller lab401) most closely matches PandwaRF's own 'Marauder Standard' tier at EUR990. PandwaRF also sells a 'Basic' tier at EUR790 (~$818) without rolling-code support, and an 'Ultimate' tier (price not published, contact-to-purchase) bundling a one-year 'Kaiju Gate Openers Pack - LEA License.' LEA stands for Law Enforcement Agency: the deepest rolling-code decryption/generation features are explicitly licensed to law enforcement rather than sold openly. The specific lab401 URL in the seed data returned HTTP 404 at time of research, suggesting that listing may have been delisted or gone out of stock.
skill_note: Designed to be deployed and left running unattended (a 'dead drop'); its rolling-code analysis output is only useful to someone who already understands RF/keyfob protocols and has (or buys) the separate Kaiju analysis software/subscription.
build_note: Sold assembled and ready to deploy; the Ultimate tier includes three band-specific antennas, a USB-C cable and a hard case.
summary: An autonomous, battery-powered sub-GHz capture device meant to be hidden near a target (a 'dead drop') and left running for extended periods, silently recording keyfob, garage-door and alarm-remote transmissions on 315/433/868/915 MHz to internal memory (256-512 captures depending on tier) for later retrieval over Bluetooth LE. It shares the broader PandwaRF ecosystem with the handheld PandwaRF Rogue Pro, but is built for unattended field collection rather than interactive handheld use.
honest_take: Read the tier structure before assuming you are buying 'rolling-code defeat': the Basic tier (EUR790) only logs fixed-code transmissions with no timestamps; genuine rolling-code cataloguing needs the Standard tier (EUR990) or above, and PandwaRF's own material is explicit that 'rolling code support' here means capturing and cataloguing transmissions for offline analysis via their separate Kaiju software, not defeating the rolling-code cryptography outright. Kaiju's most capable 'Gate Openers Pack' - with model identification and code generation - is gated behind a one-year 'LEA' (Law Enforcement Agency) license bundled only with the Ultimate tier, which strongly implies PandwaRF does not sell the strongest rolling-code-defeat features to the general public. As a covert implant this is a serious, purpose-built tool at a serious price (comparable to the handheld PandwaRF Rogue Pro plus an ongoing analysis subscription) - it is not a garage-door hacking gadget for a hobbyist, and deploying it on property or vehicles you do not own crosses from an RF-licensing question into a physical-intrusion and surveillance-law question well before the transmission-licensing one does.

name: RFQuack
firmware_note: GPL-2.0 firmware you build yourself onto a user-supplied ESP32 or Teensy (2.x/3.x/4.x) board wired to a CC1101, RF69 or nRF24L01 radio module; there is no fixed hardware design.

skill_note: You wire your own ESP32/Teensy to a CC1101/RF69/nRF24L01 module, flash the firmware yourself, and drive it from a Python shell - there is no packaged product or guided setup.
build_note: No PCB of its own; you wire off-the-shelf dev boards and radio breakout modules together over SPI and flash the RFQuack firmware.
summary: An open-source, GPL-2.0 firmware (with an accompanying academic paper) that turns a user-wired ESP32 or Teensy plus a CC1101, RF69 or nRF24L01 radio module into a Python-scriptable RF sniff/analyze/transmit tool, in the same spirit as RfCat but supporting three different radio chips including 2.4 GHz via the nRF24L01.
honest_take: This is a software project, not a device - there is nothing to buy, and the price in this database is a rough guess at the cost of one bare radio module, not a working tool. Its real comparison point is RfCat/YARD Stick One: RFQuack covers more radio chips (CC1101 and RF69 sub-GHz, plus nRF24L01 2.4 GHz in one framework) but has no equivalent to a pre-built, cased USB stick - you are entirely on your own for hardware, wiring and enclosure. Development has been quiet since its last commit in December 2024 (GitHub API rate-limited a precise 'last release' check during this research pass, but the commit date is confirmed), so expect an academic-project pace of support - it originated from a published research paper - rather than a maintained commercial product.
